target: Se me cayó el alma al suelo cuando me enteré.
english: My heart sank when I found out (lit. my soul fell to the floor).
tip: "Se me cayó el alma al suelo" – accidental se construction (se + indirect object). Literally "my soul fell to the floor on me." The "se me" removes agency.

target: El no haber estudiado lo suficiente fue lo que le costo el examen.
english: Not having studied enough was what caused him to fail the exam.
tip: 'El no haber estudiado' – an article on a verb? Spanish turns whole events into nouns with el + infinitive, where English must switch to -ing: 'not having studied'.

target: Me flipa esta serie.
english: I'm blown away by this series (lit. it flips me out).
tip: 'Me flipa' borrows English 'flip (out)' and works like gustar – the series flips YOU. Spain-only slang: perfect with friends, jarring with your boss.

target: Si no llega a ser por ese mapa, nos habríamos perdido.
english: If it hadn't been for that map, we would have gotten lost (lit. if it doesn't get to be for that map).
tip: "Si no llega a ser por" – colloquial alternative to "si no hubiera sido por" for past counterfactuals.

target: Le echaron la bronca por no haber avisado con tiempo.
english: He got told off for not having given notice in time.
tip: Echar (throw) is Spain's delivery verb for abstract things: le echaron la bronca = they literally threw the scolding at him. Very colloquial – use regañar in formal speech.

target: No fue sino despues de mucho pensarlo cuando tome la decision.
english: It wasn't until after thinking about it a lot that I made the decision.
tip: Cleft sentence: No fue sino...cuando = It wasn't until...that.

target: La fiesta es en mi casa; mi casa es grande y luminosa.
english: The party is at my house – my house is big and bright.
tip: Why es for location here? Events take ser: la fiesta es en mi casa = it takes place there. Only physical things use estar for where they are.

target: Hechas las presentaciones, comenzó la negociación.
english: Once the introductions were made, the negotiation began.
tip: No 'once they were' needed – Spanish drops it all. Participle goes first and agrees with its noun: hechas las presentaciones = the introductions (once) made.

target: El haber vivido en varios países le dio una perspectiva única.
english: Having lived in several countries gave him a unique perspective.
tip: English says 'having lived'; Spanish slaps el on an infinitive instead: el haber vivido = the-fact-of-having-lived, a noun that can be the subject.

target: Cuantos más años pasan, más se parecen los hermanos entre sí.
english: The more years go by, the more the siblings resemble each other.
tip: 'The more' can pluralize! Cuanto agrees like an adjective: cuantos más años (masc. plural years). English 'the' never changes form; cuanto matches gender and number.

target: No es sino trabajando todos juntos como lograremos superar esta crisis.
english: It is only by working together that we will overcome this crisis.
tip: No es sino + gerund + como = it is only by... that (emphatic cleft).

target: Le regalé a mi amiga un collar de plata para su cumpleaños.
english: I gave my friend a silver necklace for her birthday.
tip: Why le AND a mi amiga? Spanish doubles a named indirect object with its clitic: le regalé a mi amiga. Dropping le sounds broken, not tidy.

target: La etiqueta dice que el producto está fabricado en España con materiales importados.
english: The label says the product is manufactured in Spain with imported materials.
tip: Why está, not es? Está fabricado reports the product's finished state; es fabricado would narrate the act of making it. Labels describe results, so estar.

target: Mi abuela cumplió ochenta y siete años el mes pasado.
english: My grandmother turned eighty-seven last month.
tip: Birthdays aren't 'turned' in Spanish – they're completed: cumplió ochenta y siete años = she 'fulfilled' 87 years. That's why it's ¡feliz cumpleaños!

target: Ella es madrina de mi hija desde que nació.
english: She's been my daughter's godmother since my daughter was born.
tip: English needs 'has been godmother'; Spanish uses plain present: es madrina desde que nació. If it started back then and still holds, present tense covers it.

target: Se me pasó por alto ese detalle en el contrato.
english: I overlooked that detail in the contract.
tip: Spanish deflects blame with se: se me pasó por alto = the detail 'slipped past' on its own – me just marks the bystander it happened to. Not 'I missed it.'

target: Las personas a quienes les conté el secreto son de confianza.
english: The people I told the secret to are trustworthy.
tip: Spanish doubles the object: a quienes LES conté – les repeats the 'to whom' already stated. Redundant to English ears, expected in Spanish.

target: El jefe nos dio carta blanca para redisenar la pagina web.
english: The boss gave us a blank check to redesign the website.
tip: English writes a blank check; Spanish hands you carta blanca – a 'white letter': a blank page to fill in however you like. Same total freedom, no money image.

target: Lo difícil no es empezar, sino mantener la constancia a lo largo del tiempo.
english: The hard part isn't starting, but maintaining consistency over time.
tip: Two 'but's: pero adds a contrast, sino corrects after a negative. No es empezar, SINO mantener – whenever you mean 'not X but rather Y', only sino works.

target: Lo paradójico del asunto es que quienes más se quejan son quienes menos trabajan.
english: The paradox of the matter is that those who complain the most are those who work the least.
tip: No 'the paradoxical thing' needed: lo paradójico turns any adjective straight into an abstract noun. Lo works on all of them – lo bueno, lo raro, lo difícil.

target: Mi tía vive en el extranjero desde hace cinco años.
english: My aunt has been living abroad for five years.
tip: Five years and still counting? English needs "has been living"; Spanish uses plain present: "vive en el extranjero desde hace cinco años" – still true means present tense.

target: Se nos pinchó una rueda en medio de la carretera.
english: We got a flat tire in the middle of the road.
tip: Nobody's to blame: "Se nos pinchó una rueda" = the tire "punctured itself on us." Accidental se recasts mishaps as things that happen TO you, not things you did.

target: La lengua española es hablada por más de quinientos millones de personas.
english: The Spanish language is spoken by more than five hundred million people.
tip: "Es hablada" is grammatical but bookish: ser + participle passives live in print. In conversation Spanish prefers the se-passive – "se habla español."

target: No solo habla español, sino que también domina el francés.
english: Not only does he speak Spanish, but he also masters French.
tip: Why the que? Because a conjugated verb (domina) follows. With a bare noun, sino stands alone: no café, sino té. Full clause after sino = sino que, every time.

target: Lo siento, metí la pata; no debí haber dicho eso.
english: I'm sorry, I put my foot in it. I shouldn't have said that.
tip: "Metí la pata" = literally "I stuck my paw in." Spanish's go-to phrase for a social blunder – and it's always pata (an animal's leg), never pierna (a human one).

target: Firmado el contrato, ambas partes se comprometieron a cumplir los plazos.
english: Once the contract was signed, both parties committed to meeting the deadlines.
tip: "Firmado el contrato" – no "once" or "was" in sight. Fronting a bare participle means "once X was done." Formal shorthand beloved of contracts and news reports.

target: Con que los niños se porten bien en la cena, me conformo.
english: As long as the kids behave at dinner, I'll be satisfied.
tip: "Con que" here isn't "with what": con que + subjunctive ("se porten bien") means "as long as" – the bare minimum you'll settle for, hence "me conformo."

target: La sudadera verde claro es muy cómoda para estar en casa.
english: The light green hoodie is very comfortable for being at home.
tip: Why not verde clara to agree with la sudadera? Compound shades like 'verde claro' are frozen – add claro or oscuro and the color stops agreeing entirely.

target: Si no hubiera aprendido a manejar, no podría hacer este viaje.
english: If I hadn't learned to drive, I couldn't make this trip.
tip: Past cause, present result: 'hubiera aprendido' (back then) pairs with 'no podría' (today) – Spanish mixes conditional timelines when a past event still affects the present.

target: Habría ido si me hubieran invitado.
english: I would have gone if they'd invited me.
tip: Tempted by 'si me habrían invitado'? Spanish bans the conditional after si – the if-half takes 'hubieran invitado'; only the result gets 'habría ido'.
